title: I Survived 100 Days as an Elephant Who Lost Her Family
description: Animal Secrets #26 — What if you were a young Sri Lankan elephant whose grandmother dies and whose family breaks apart? A Day 1 to Day 100 survival story, but every number is real. This week (12 Nov 2026) the journal Science put Udawalawe's elephants on its cover: after 12 years, big families of 14 had shattered into groups of fewer than four.
tags: i survived 100 days as an elephant
what if you were an elephant

scenes.say: Can you hear that? That's mud, sucking my legs down. I'm stuck.
It's night. There are lights and shouting people all around this rice field. And my sister is calling me from the dark.
I'm a young Sri Lankan elephant. Okay, so this is a story, a what if. But every number in it is real.
How did I end up here, alone, sinking? And who do I find by the end, on Day 100? Let me take you back. Day 1.

scenes.label: Udawalawe, Sri Lanka
scenes.say: Day 1. Udawalawe National Park, southern Sri Lanka. Grass, scrub, a big lake, and my whole family.
Fourteen of us. Mothers, aunts, cousins, babies. And in front, always in front, my grandmother.
Here's the thing about us. Eating is basically our full-time job. About three quarters of every single day.

scenes.label: 150 kg a day
scenes.say: An adult can eat up to 150 kilos of plants a day and drink around 190 liters of water.
Why so much? Because we only absorb about 44 percent of what we eat. The rest just passes through.
Which, honestly, the dung beetles love. Our droppings are their whole world.
And my grandmother? She's the one who remembers where all that food and water is. Every path. Every season.
Remember that. It's going to matter a lot more than I knew.
Day 6. Bath day at the water. My favorite day.
We have no sweat glands to cool off. So we throw water and mud all over our backs.

scenes.label: 5-10x more water
scenes.say: Our skin is covered in tiny cracks. Scientists found those cracks hold five to ten times more water than smooth skin.
So the mud stays on. It blocks the sun and the biting bugs, like sunscreen you wear for hours.
The water buffalo don't even look up. They've seen us do this a thousand times.
A peacock screams from the bank. My little cousin, three years old, tries to chase it and falls on his face.
Everyone rumbles. That's our laugh, kind of. I think this is the best family in the world.
A grey heron stands on one leg, watching us splash. Even it looks bored. Life is easy. For now.
Day 11. But something's wrong with the grass. There's less of it every year.
This shrub is called lantana. It's one of the worst invasive plants on Earth, and we can't eat it.

scenes.label: 2,650 hectares
scenes.say: In this park, it has spread over about 2,650 hectares. Studies show the grassland here shrank between 2005 and 2019.
Less grass means longer walks. Longer walks mean tired babies. And tired babies slow everybody down.
And we're not the only hungry ones. Spotted deer, buffalo, even cattle all graze the same shrinking grass.
That evening, the ground hums. A deep sound, too low for human ears. Another family is talking to us.

scenes.label: 2+ miles away
scenes.say: Our rumbles are infrasound. Other elephants can understand them more than two miles away.
Grandma lifts her trunk, listens, and answers. She knows exactly who it is. I don't. I never learned.
Day 18. Grandmother is walking slower. She stops more. She eats less.
Tonight she lies down under a tree, and in the morning, she doesn't get up. She was very, very old.
Nobody leaves. We stand around her for hours. We touch her with our trunks. Nobody makes a sound.
I don't know how long we stay. I just know that something in the family breaks that day.
And here's the scary part. All the maps were in her head. Now who knows where the water is?
Day 22. My aunt walks east. My mother's cousin walks south. Nobody agrees. And the family splits.
This is not just my story. This exact thing was on the cover of the journal Science, this month.

scenes.label: 443 elephants, 12 years
scenes.say: Scientists followed 443 female elephants right here in Udawalawe for 12 years.
At the start, they counted 20 groups, about 14 elephants each. Just like my family.

scenes.label: 20 groups → 37
scenes.say: By the end, more than two thirds of the elephants had died or left. And the groups had shattered.
37 groups. Fewer than four elephants in each, on average. They called it a tipping point.
And that's me now. Me, my older sister, and my three-year-old cousin. Three. That's my whole family.

scenes.label: Dry season
scenes.say: Day 29. The dry season. The waterhole where Grandma always took us? Cracked mud. Nothing.
My sister guesses left. I guess right. We're both wrong. We walk all day and find only dust.
We pass the same termite mound three times. Three. We're walking in circles, and the sun is brutal.
Scientists saw this in Tanzania too. In a terrible drought in 1993, calf deaths jumped from about 2 to 20 percent.
The families that survived best were the ones that walked out and found new water. Led by older, wiser mothers.
We don't have one. My cousin's skin is dusty and his trunk hangs low. So I make a choice.
I follow my nose. Elephants can smell water. And somewhere, far off, I smell something green.
Quick thing: if you're liking this story, subscribe. One animal secret a day. Now, let's keep walking.
Day 34. The smell leads to the edge of the park. And there's a line I've never seen. A wire.

scenes.label: It bites
scenes.say: It buzzes. My sister touches it with her trunk and jumps back, squealing. It bites.

scenes.label: 4,500+ km of fence
scenes.say: Sri Lanka has built more than 4,500 kilometers of these fences to keep elephants and farms apart.
Most give a scary shock. But illegal ones can kill. In just 7 months of 2025, 38 elephants died from electrocution.
We back away. Behind the wire, I can see bananas. And rice. And people's houses.
Day 40. A huge male shows up at night. His face is dripping, and he smells strong. He's in musth.
Musth is when big bulls get flooded with hormones. They get restless and fight. Even we keep our distance.

scenes.label: 90% no tusks
scenes.say: Fun fact? Over 90 percent of Sri Lankan males have no tusks at all. This one doesn't either.
But he does know something we don't. Where the fence is broken. And he's walking right toward it.
On the way, a leopard watches us from a rock, eyes glowing. My sister steps in front of my cousin. It slips away.
Day 47. We follow him through the gap. My heart is pounding. The bananas are right there.
I pull down one plant, then two. It's the best thing I've eaten in weeks. Then a loud bang.
A firecracker. Farmers use them to chase us away. Lights, shouting, dogs barking. We run.
Wild boar raid these farms too. Deer and porcupines too. But nothing scares a farmer like an elephant.
I get it, though. For them, one night of us can wipe out a whole season of rice.
And this fight is getting worse. In 2011, 255 elephants were killed in Sri Lanka. In 2023, 488.

scenes.label: 184 people
scenes.say: And that same year, 184 people died too. Nobody wins this war. Not us, not them.
Day 55. We're back inside the park, but there's almost nothing to eat. So we try another way out.
Two long metal lines on the ground. They're warm from the sun. My cousin stops right on top of them to sniff.
Then the ground starts shaking. A low horn. A light, coming fast.
My sister shoves him off the tracks with her head. The train roars past, so close I feel the wind.

scenes.label: 13 hit by trains
scenes.say: Trains hit 13 elephants in Sri Lanka in just seven months of 2025. That was almost 14.
We don't sleep that night. We stand together under the moon, touching trunks, shaking.
Fireflies blink in the grass like nothing happened. My cousin finally dozes, leaning on my leg.
Day 63. And now you know how I got here. Night. Rice field. Me, stuck.
The field was flooded, and I walked in too fast. The mud sucked my back legs down. My leg hurts.
The harder I pull, the deeper I go. My sister rumbles from the trees, but she can't come any closer.
This month, this exact thing happened in Sri Lanka. An eight-year-old elephant fell into a muddy paddy field.
Wildlife officers and villagers lifted her out together. So, what happens to me?
Headlights. A truck. Men in uniforms with ropes and straps. Wildlife officers.
They work for hours. They yell at the crowd to step back. Then, slowly, the mud lets go.
I'm out. My leg is swollen, and a vet treats it. But when I turn around, my cousin is gone.
Day 66. The officers found him alone, wandering at the forest edge. Too small to make it by himself.
They took him to a place called the Elephant Transit Home, right inside Udawalawe.
It opened in 1995, the first of its kind in the world. It raises orphaned elephants and sends them back to the wild.

scenes.label: 186 released
scenes.say: 442 orphans have come through it. 186 have been released so far. More than anywhere else on Earth.
The babies get milk every three hours. Keepers barely touch them, so they stay wild.
He'll go free at around five or six. Years from now. I won't see him for a long, long time.
That night I hear jackals calling, and I keep turning around, looking for a little shape that isn't there.
So it's just me and my sister now. Two. And two is way too small for an elephant.
Day 71. So we do what Grandma did. Every evening, we rumble. And we listen.

scenes.label: 2 km day, 10 km night
scenes.say: Here's a secret. Our calls travel much farther at night. One study estimated about 2 kilometers by day, almost 10 by night.
Night after night, nothing. Just frogs and wind. Then, on Day 78, someone answers.
Day 80. We find them by the lake. Six young elephants. No mothers. No grandmother. Just kids, like us.
And then I smell it. Milk formula. These are orphans from the Transit Home, released together as a small herd.
They release them in mini herds of four to a dozen. They learn to be wild together.
Will they let us in? Asian elephant groups are pretty flexible. Members can come and go, even unrelated ones.
The tallest girl walks up and puts her trunk in my mouth. That's a greeting. That's a yes.
They show me their spots. A muddy wallow, a fallen fig tree, a monitor lizard that hisses at everybody.
Day 88. New problem. The orphans are brave, but they don't know this land. Nobody taught them.
The waterhole is dry again. They look lost. And everyone turns around and looks at me.
There's one more pool nearby. But a mugger crocodile is lying in it, and the orphans won't go near it.
Me? I'm not a grandmother. But then I remember Day 6. The bath. The river. Grandma's path.
So I walk. Past the dead tree. Down the old trail. And there it is. Water, still flowing.
Turns out I learned more than I thought. I just had to be the one who remembers.
Day 95. The ground hums again. A big family is coming. Fifteen, maybe more. With a very old leader.
The orphans bunch up, scared. Strangers can mean trouble. But the old leader stops and listens to me.

scenes.label: Old = wise
scenes.say: Studies show older matriarchs are much better at telling familiar voices from strangers.
She rumbles. Long and low. And I know that voice. She used to visit my grandmother.
Day 100. We walk into the morning together. Her family, the orphans, my sister, and me.
Is it my old family? No. Grandma's gone. My cousin is growing up somewhere else. That doesn't come back.
But scientists say this is the key. Families stay strong only if they can replace the bonds they lose.
That's how I survived 100 days. Not by being the strongest. By letting new ones in.
Real elephants in Sri Lanka are living this story right now. Would you have trusted the strangers? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: A Baby Elephant Is Sinking in a Rice Field
short.description: A young Sri Lankan elephant stuck in a flooded paddy field at night. Full Day 1 to Day 100 story on the channel.

scenes.say: Nobody can pull me out of this rice field. The mud won't let go.
I'm a young Sri Lankan elephant. My grandmother died, my family split up, and I walked out of the park looking for food.
This field was flooded. My back legs sank, and the harder I pull, the deeper I go.
Sri Lanka loses more elephants to conflict with people than any country on Earth. In 2023, 488 elephants died, and 184 people too.
Then headlights. Wildlife officers with ropes. This month, a real eight-year-old elephant was lifted out of a paddy field just like this.
So do I get out? Full story on my channel. Because right now, nobody can pull me out of this rice field, and the mud won't let go.
